name: Avoiding soy ("soy boy" meta)

lead: Followers of the soy-avoidance meta skip soy foods out of concern that phytoestrogens lower testosterone or soften male features, aiming to keep masculine muscle and looks. The "soy boy" insult grew from this idea.

Soy isoflavones resemble estradiol and act on estrogen receptors, which is the basis of the concern. Wikipedia reports that a 2021 meta-analysis found neither soy nor isoflavone intake affects male reproductive hormones in healthy individuals, and a 2021 review concluded soyfoods do not warrant classification as endocrine disruptors. The topic is still described as under study.

paras: People read ingredient labels and cut out tofu, soy milk, soy protein and processed foods containing soy, usually replacing them with other protein sources. It is a long-term dietary habit.

Reference texts report no hormonal harm from soy in healthy men, and some studies report mixed findings on sperm measures. Cutting soy can narrow protein choices, and soy infant formula has narrow pediatric indications per the American Academy of Pediatrics. The term also functions as a political insult.

angle.text: Skipping soy aims to avoid phytoestrogens that followers believe lower testosterone and soften male features. Meta-analyses report no effect of soy on male reproductive hormones in healthy men, so the appearance link rests largely on forum belief.

lead: Avoiding soy is a dietary practice in which men limit soy foods, such as tofu, soy milk, edamame, soy protein isolate and soy-derived additives, because they believe soy isoflavones lower testosterone or add estrogenic effects. Followers connect this to appearance: they hope to keep a leaner, harder-looking physique, easier muscle gain, a more defined jaw and a less "soft" face [1].

The practice is entangled with "soy boy", an online insult for men seen as lacking masculine traits. The term draws on the fact that soy contains isoflavones, plant compounds structurally similar to estradiol, and it went viral on social media in February 2017 [1]. The insult and the diet question are separate things: some people cut soy for a physique goal, others for allergy reasons, and others use the word purely as political or cultural slang.

Published research on the hormonal question includes two meta-analyses of clinical trials, in 2010 and an expanded update in 2021, both concluding that soy protein or isoflavone intake did not change reproductive hormones in men [2][3]. Reference texts describe phytoestrogen effects in men as still under study, and a 2021 review concluded soyfoods and isoflavones do not warrant classification as endocrine disruptors [1].

paras: The practice ranges from skipping soy milk and tofu to reading labels to avoid soy protein isolate, soy lecithin and soybean oil in packaged foods. Because soy appears in many processed and restaurant foods, thorough avoidance involves checking ingredient lists, a point also made in allergy guidance [4].

In fitness and looksmaxxing circles the reasoning is usually framed around hormones: testosterone supports muscle, leanness and a masculine face and body, and estrogen-like compounds are thought to work against that. Followers often combine soy avoidance with other diet and lifestyle steps aimed at the same goal, such as higher protein intake, meat and egg-centred eating, and avoiding other perceived endocrine disruptors.

"Soy boy" is a derogatory online term, typically aimed at left-leaning men, built on the claim that soy phytoestrogens feminize men [1]. Its modern origin is unclear. It has been attributed to 4chan's /pol/ board, to the YouTube commentator James Allsup and to Mike Cernovich, and Alex Jones, Roosh Valizadeh and Paul Joseph Watson are cited as popularisers [1]. A license plate reading "#1 SOY BOY" appeared in a 2008 pop music video, an earlier appearance of the phrase [1].

In February 2017, after protesters disrupted Shia LaBeouf's anti-Trump art installation "He Will Not Divide Us" while carrying dairy milk, the hashtags #MilkTwitter and #SoyBoy spread widely on Twitter [1]. Commentators on the far right also popularised the terms "soy face" and "Soylent grin" for an exaggerated facial expression they attributed to low testosterone, a reference to a soy-based meal replacement drink [1]. A 1970s article claiming soy disrupts hormone balance is credited with starting soy's negative reputation, though Wikipedia flags that source as possibly unreliable [1].

Wikipedia also places the idea in a longer history in which dairy was credited with Northern European success while plant-based diets in India and China were described as making people weak or effeminate [1].

Proponents say soy isoflavones bind estrogen receptors, nudge the testosterone-to-estrogen balance and produce softer features, lower drive and harder fat loss. Some describe a "soy face" with a softer jaw and a less defined look [1]. Wikipedia notes these claims have been made mainly by conspiracy-oriented commentators [1].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums the claim is often stated as general hormone hygiene, and men who report feeling better after dropping soy usually cite energy, digestion or body composition. Forum posts that use "soy boy" are more often insults than discussion of diet, and many of the threads in which the phrase appears are about politics rather than nutrition.

Soy isoflavones are phytoestrogens that resemble estradiol and can bind estrogen receptors, which is why early research raised endocrine-disruptor concerns [1]. Later work was more reassuring. A 2010 meta-analysis in Fertility and Sterility by Hamilton-Reeves and colleagues reported that clinical studies showed no effect of soy protein or isoflavones on reproductive hormones in men [2]. A 2021 expanded and updated meta-analysis in Reproductive Toxicology by Reed, Camargo, Hamilton-Reeves, Kurzer and Messina reached the same conclusion for healthy men [3].

Wikipedia's phytoestrogens article reports that some isoflavone studies found positive effects on sperm concentration, count or motility, while dietary intakes above typical Asian levels did not affect estrogen, testosterone, sperm or semen amounts in the Linus Pauling Institute's summary. A 2018 review by Nassan and colleagues found no link between phytoestrogens and male fertility, and a 2021 review by Messina and colleagues concluded soyfoods and isoflavones do not warrant classification as endocrine disruptors. The Linus Pauling Institute still describes the effect of phytoestrogens on male reproductive physiology as under study.
Higher soy intake is associated with lower prostate cancer risk, and a 2025 meta-analysis found plant-based diets do not compromise muscular strength, according to Wikipedia [1].

The two meta-analyses above pooled randomised and controlled clinical studies of soy protein or isoflavones and measured testosterone and other reproductive hormones in men, reporting no significant effect [2][3]. Smaller studies cited in reference texts examined sperm parameters, with some reporting improvements and others none. Gynecomastia has many recognised causes, including drugs, obesity, liver disease, alcohol and hypogonadism [5].

sections.h: Allergy and other reasons to avoid soy
paras: Soy is among the eight most common food allergens, with about 0.3% of the general population affected, and reactions range from hives to anaphylaxis [4]. People with confirmed soy allergy avoid soy ingredients for that reason, which is a separate motive from the hormonal one. Some people also limit soy for digestive reasons or personal preference.

In looksmaxxing communities, soy avoidance sits among testosterone-focused habits, alongside sleep, lifting, sunlight and diet choices. Discussion often links it to facial aesthetics, with the idea that hormones shape jaw, brow and facial leanness. The term "soy boy" is used as an insult across forums, including bodybuilding sites, often with no connection to diet at all [1].

lore.intro: Online, soy avoidance is discussed both as a physique and testosterone habit and as political slang; the two uses are often mixed [1].
